lead: A flat belt is a loop of flexible material that grips a pulley by friction over part of its rim. The driver pulls the tight side; the slack side returns. The two tensions are tied by T₁/T₂ = e^(μθ), so the belt can pull only as hard as friction allows. Design means choosing a width b so that the tight-side tension plus centrifugal tension stays below the safe strength σbt. Flat belts drive line shafts, conveyors, and small machines where shafts are far apart and some slip is acceptable.
prereq: You need 6.1 for belt materials, thickness and density, and Unit 1 for direct stress and factor of safety.

sections.h3: Grip and the arc of contact

blocks.text: A flat belt transmits power only where it touches the pulley. The driver pulls the tight side and feeds the slack side. The arc of contact is the angle over which the belt touches a pulley. The smaller pulley has the smaller arc, so it sets the friction limit.

Use d and D for the small and large pulley diameters in metres, C for the centre distance in metres, and N₁, N₂ for speeds in rpm. Ignoring slip, N₁d = N₂D. With slip fraction s, N₂ = N₁(d/D)(1 − s); s is the fraction of belt speed lost.

blocks.where: θd is the arc of contact on the smaller pulley of an open belt, in degrees; d and D are pulley diameters; C is the centre distance.
θd is the arc of contact on the smaller pulley of a crossed belt, in degrees; the belt crosses between the pulleys.

blocks.text: Convert θd to radians before using e^(μθ). Belt length for an open drive is L = 2C + π(D + d)/2 + (D − d)²/(4C). For a crossed drive, L = 2C + π(D + d)/2 + (D + d)²/(4C).

Let T₁ be the tight-side tension and T₂ the slack-side tension that produce friction, in N. The centrifugal tension is Tc = m v², where m is the belt mass per metre in kg/m and v is belt speed in m/s. For width b in metres, thickness t in metres and density ρ in kg/m³, m = ρbt.

blocks.where: μ is the coefficient of friction; θ is the arc of contact on the smaller pulley in radians; e = 2.718.

blocks.text: The safe tension is T = σbt, where σ is the safe stress in N/m². The tight side carries T₁ plus Tc, so T₁ + Tc ≤ T. Power is P = (T₁ − T₂)v. Initial tension is T₀ = (T₁ + T₂)/2 + Tc.

At fixed T and μθ, P = (1 − 1/e^(μθ))(T − m v²)v. Differentiate with respect to v. Maximum power occurs when Tc = m v² = T/3, so v = √(T/(3m)). For T = 1000 N and m = 0.6 kg/m, v = √(1000/(3×0.6)) = 23.6 m/s. Above this speed, Tc grows as v² and the useful grip falls.

items: Find v from the smaller pulley: v = πdN₁/60.
Find θd for the smaller pulley and convert it to radians.
Find the driving tension difference: T₁ − T₂ = P/v.
Solve T₁ and T₂ using the ratio T₁/T₂ = e^(μθ).
Compute m = ρbt and Tc = m v². Use b in metres here.
Set T₁ + Tc = σbt and solve for b.
Round b up to a standard width. Check T₀ and the pulley face width.

blocks.text: Creep is the stretch on the tight side and contraction on the slack side. It makes the driven pulley lag slightly even with good friction. Slip is gross sliding when T₁/T₂ exceeds e^(μθ). Both reduce the velocity ratio. A flat belt is chosen when some slip is acceptable and the shafts are far apart.

figure.caption: Transmitted power rises to a peak near 24 m/s where Tc = T/3, then falls because centrifugal tension uses up the grip.

series.name: T v − m v³, T = 1000 N, m = 0.6 kg/m

examples.question: A 15 kW motor at 1440 rpm drives a line shaft at 480 rpm through an open flat belt. The pulley diameters are 200 mm and 600 mm, the centre distance is 2 m, μ = 0.3, belt thickness is 10 mm, density is 1000 kg/m³, and safe stress is 2.5 N/mm². Find the belt width.
steps: Check velocity ratio without slip: N₁d = 1440 × 0.200 = 288; N₂D = 480 × 0.600 = 288. The speeds are consistent with these diameters.
Driving tension difference: T₁ − T₂ = P/v = 15000/15.08 = 994.72 N.
Belt mass per metre: m = ρbt. With b in mm, t = 0.010 m, ρ = 1000 kg/m³: m = 1000 × (b/1000) × 0.010 = 0.010b kg/m. Tc = m v² = 0.010b × 15.08² = 2.27b N.
Safe tension: T = σbt = 2.5 × b × 10 = 25b N (σ = 2.5 N/mm², t = 10 mm).
Strength condition: T₁ + Tc = T → 1696.89 + 2.27b = 25b → 22.73b = 1696.89 → b = 74.67 mm.
Take the next standard width: b = 80 mm.
examples.answer: The required belt width is 74.67 mm; use a standard 80 mm wide flat belt.
examples.check:
import math
P = 15000.0
N1 = 1440.0
d = 0.2
D = 0.6
C = 2.0
mu = 0.3
t = 0.01
rho = 1000.0
sigma = 2.5e6
v = math.pi * d * N1 / 60
theta_deg = 180 - 2 * math.degrees(math.asin((D - d) / (2 * C)))
theta = math.radians(theta_deg)
k = math.exp(mu * theta)
dT = P / v
T2 = dT / (k - 1)
T1 = dT + T2
m_per_mm = rho * t / 1000.0
Tc_coeff = m_per_mm * v**2
T_coeff = sigma * t / 1000.0
b = T1 / (T_coeff - Tc_coeff)
print(round(v, 2))
print(round(theta_deg, 2))
print(round(theta, 2))
print(round(k, 2))
print(round(dT, 2))
print(round(T2, 2))
print(round(T1, 2))
print(round(Tc_coeff, 2))
print(round(T_coeff, 2))
print(round(b, 2))

traps: Using 180° as the arc of contact. Use the smaller pulley's arc; for an open belt it is less than 180°.
Feeding degrees into e^(μθ). Convert θ to radians first.
Forgetting centrifugal tension Tc. At high speed it can use a large part of the safe tension.
Mixing millimetres and metres in m = ρbt. Use b and t in metres for m, then convert the answer.
Treating T₁ alone as the safe tension. The strength limit is T₁ + Tc = σbt.

quiz.q: Write the formula for centrifugal tension Tc and define each term.
quiz.a: Tc = m v²; m is the belt mass per metre in kg/m and v is the belt speed in m/s.

quiz.q: Why does maximum power occur at Tc = T/3?
quiz.a: For fixed T and μθ, P = (1 − 1/e^(μθ))(T − m v²)v. Differentiating gives T − 3m v² = 0, so m v² = T/3. Below this speed the belt is too slow; above it, centrifugal tension uses too much of the safe strength.

quiz.q: An open belt has d = 150 mm, D = 450 mm and C = 1.5 m. Find the arc of contact on the small pulley in radians.
A flat belt drive transmits the same power at a very low speed and at a very high speed. Explain why both need a wider belt than the speed for maximum power.
quiz.a: At low speed, P = (T₁ − T₂)v needs a large tension difference, so T₁ is high. At high speed, Tc = m v² is high, so the useful T₁ is reduced. At v = √(T/(3m)) the product is largest.

quiz.q: For T = 1200 N and m = 0.5 kg/m, find the belt speed for maximum power.
Distinguish creep from slip in a belt drive.
quiz.a: Creep is elastic stretch and contraction of the belt as it moves from slack to tight side; it is always present. Slip is gross sliding when friction is insufficient; it is avoidable by design.

quiz.q: Why is the arc on the smaller pulley used in design, not the larger pulley's arc?
quiz.a: Friction capacity depends on the smallest arc. The smaller pulley has θd less than 180° in an open drive, so it governs e^(μθ). If the belt does not slip there, it will not slip on the larger pulley.

quiz.q: A belt transmits 10 kW at 12 m/s. e^(μθ) = 2.0. Find T₁ and T₂.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern flat belts are often polyurethane or aramid-corded and run at high speed with small pulleys. Synchronous belts replace friction with teeth, so they do not slip and do not need the e^(μθ) limit. Conveyor belts add idlers, take-ups and cleaning systems, which change the design from a simple two-pulley problem. Search 'flat belt power rating', 'synchronous belt', or 'conveyor belt design' to go further.
